explanations.explanation: Jerusalem is right, friend. Verse 13 says John left them at Perga to return there. The text doesn't tell us why he went, so I'm not guessing out loud. I'll just say that when a teammate heads home mid-journey, the rest of the crew still has dough to roll.

Damascus is a city, but it's not where John goes. Acts 13:13 says he left them at Perga to return to Jerusalem. The text sticks to that one destination and so do I. Mixing up cities happens to the best of us, and I once mixed up salt and sugar.
Tarsus is a city too, but John doesn't head there. Verse 13 says he returned to Jerusalem. That's the only place the text names for him. Good guess on a real city, friend, but the map says Jerusalem.

I get the thought, since visitors usually sit tight and nod. But look at verse 15. After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the leaders send word: “Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak.” That's an invitation, friend, not a shush. Nobody's getting a finger to the lips in that synagogue.

False is right. The leaders don't say a word about staying quiet. They send word in verse 15: “Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak.” Two visitors just sat down, and they got handed the floor. I've been to places where visitors got handed a pamphlet instead.

Yes, a word of encouragement. The leaders say, “…if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak.” They send word to the two visitors after the reading from the Law and the Prophets. Notice they ask politely, and Paul takes them up on it. Wait until you see how much encouragement fits in one sermon.

That's a sensible guess, because Jerusalem was just mentioned in verse 13. But the leaders never ask for a report. Verse 15 says they ask for “a word of encouragement for the people.” Nobody wants a status update on the Sabbath, friend.

The reading already happened, though. Verse 15 says this invitation comes after the reading from the Law and the Prophets. What the leaders ask for next is “a word of encouragement for the people.” So no scroll for the guests, just their own words.

explanations.answer: Men of Israel and Gentiles who fear God
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says, “Men of Israel and you Gentiles who fear God, listen to me!” (Acts 13:16). So he's got two groups in one room, and he talks to both at once. That's a big crowd to open with, and he doesn't flinch.

explanations.answer: Priests and Levites from the temple
explanations.explanation: Nope, no temple staff gets called out here. Paul's opening words in verse 16 are “Men of Israel and you Gentiles who fear God, listen to me!” He's speaking in a synagogue, and he names who he sees there. Priests and Levites would be a fun guess if the text agreed, friend.

Those are two groups people know from elsewhere in Scripture, but Paul doesn't name them here. He opens in Acts 13:16 with “Men of Israel and you Gentiles who fear God, listen to me!” Those are the two groups he calls out. I like how you went for a matched pair, though.

True. Paul says in verse 18, “He endured their conduct for about forty years in the wilderness.” Forty years, friend. I've had a batch of cookies that I stared at for forty minutes and thought I'd lose my mind.

That's not what the text says. Acts 13:18 reads, “He endured their conduct for about forty years in the wilderness.” So Paul does say it, and he says forty years. Forty is a long stretch of patience, and Paul puts it right in the story.

Judges is right. Verse 20 says, “After this, God gave them judges until the time of Samuel the prophet.” Paul runs through a lot of history fast, and judges are one stop on the way. Keep that word handy, because the king comes right after.

Generals sounds like it fits a story with seven nations and a lot of land. But Paul says God gave them judges in Acts 13:20, until the time of Samuel the prophet. The word is judges. It's a fair guess, friend, and I'd give you a cookie for effort.

Governors sounds official, and I respect that. But Acts 13:20 says God gave them judges until the time of Samuel the prophet. So the word in the blank is judges. Samuel is the prophet Paul points to as the next marker in the story.

David son of Jesse is right. Paul says God testified about him: “I have found David son of Jesse a man after My own heart; he will carry out My will in its entirety.” (Acts 13:22). That's God's own testimony about a king. I'd frame that on my bakery wall if somebody said it about me.

Jonathan was Saul's son (1 Samuel 13:16), so I see why he came to mind. But the text says God removed Saul and raised up David son of Jesse. Verse 22 has God saying, “I have found David son of Jesse a man after My own heart…” So the king in this verse is David.

Samuel is in this passage, but as a prophet, not the king. Verse 20 names him as the prophet whose time the judges lasted until. The king in verse 22 is “David son of Jesse.” Samuel's father was Elkanah (1 Samuel 1:19, 20), so you've got your sons and fathers all lined up, friend, just the wrong one.

David is right. Paul says in verse 23, “From the descendants of this man, God has brought to Israel the Savior Jesus, as He promised.” The man right before that verse is David. So the Savior comes from David's line, and Paul says it plainly.

Saul comes up just before David, so I see how he got stuck in your head. But Paul says God removed Saul in verse 22 and raised up David. Then verse 23 says, “From the descendants of this man…” and that man is David. Saul gets the shorter end of this sermon.

Samuel is mentioned earlier in the sermon, so he's easy to grab. But the descendants Paul talks about in verse 23 belong to the man God testified about, David son of Jesse. Samuel was named only as the prophet whose time the judges lasted until. Close, friend, but David is the one.

It sounds like a big claim, but it's the other way around. John says, “I am not that One.” Then he points ahead: “But there is One coming after me whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.” (Acts 13:25). So John is pointing away from himself, not at himself.

False is right. In Acts 13:25 John says, “Who do you suppose I am? I am not that One.” He says the One coming after him is someone whose sandals he isn't worthy to untie. That's John making it clear he isn't the main event.

Pilate is right. Verse 28 says that though they found no ground for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have Him executed. It's a heavy line, and I think it hurts a little to read. Paul says it plainly, so I will too.

Herod is a name that shows up in other parts of the story, but Paul doesn't use it here. Acts 13:28 says they asked Pilate to have Jesus executed. It's a heavy verse, so I'll keep this one short. The name in the blank is Pilate.

Caiaphas was the high priest (Matthew 26:3), so he's a name people know from this part of the story. But Paul doesn't name him in this verse. Acts 13:28 says they asked Pilate to have Jesus executed. It's a heavy moment, friend, so I'll keep it simple: the answer is Pilate.

True. Verse 31 says that for many days He was seen by those who had accompanied Him from Galilee to Jerusalem. Paul adds, “They are now His witnesses to our people.” These aren't strangers passing along a rumor, friend. They're the ones who traveled with Him.

That's not how Paul tells it. Acts 13:31 says that for many days He was seen by those who had accompanied Him from Galilee to Jerusalem. Then Paul says, “They are now His witnesses to our people.” So there are plenty of eyes on it, not just one or two.

explanations.answer: It was buried and saw decay
explanations.explanation: Right. Verse 36 says David “fell asleep. His body was buried with his fathers and saw decay.” Paul sets that next to Jesus, who did not see decay (Acts 13:37). David served God's purpose in his own generation, and Paul tells us how his story ended, plain as flour.

explanations.answer: It was taken up to heaven
explanations.explanation: That's a big ending, but it's not the one Paul tells. Verse 36 says David fell asleep, “His body was buried with his fathers and saw decay.” Paul uses that to set up a contrast in verse 37 with the One God raised. So David's body stays in the buried column.

explanations.answer: It was never buried at all
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite in verse 36. David “fell asleep. His body was buried with his fathers and saw decay.” So he was buried, with his fathers. That's what makes verse 37 land, where Paul says the One God raised did not see decay.

Believes is right. Paul says, “Through Him everyone who believes is justified from everything from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses.” (Acts 13:39). Notice the word everyone. That's a wide door, friend, and Paul throws it open.

Obeying sounds like a natural fit, since people love a checklist. But Paul says in verse 39 that through Jesus “everyone who believes is justified” from what the law of Moses couldn't justify them from. The word in the blank is believes. I've got a long list of things I can't do, and this verse is good news for people like me.

Fasting is a real thing people do, but it isn't the word here. Acts 13:39 says, “Through Him everyone who believes is justified…” So the blank is believes. Nothing in that verse asks you to skip a meal, though I'd never tell you to skip a cookie.

explanations.answer: They'd never believe it if told
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 41 says, “For I am doing a work in your days that you would never believe, even if someone told you.” That's the warning to scoffers, and Paul ends the sermon on it. It's a serious closing, so I'll leave it serious.

explanations.answer: They'd see it and turn back
explanations.explanation: That's a hopeful reading, but it isn't what the verse says. Acts 13:41 says, “…a work in your days that you would never believe, even if someone told you.” So the warning is about unbelief, not turning back. I'd love a happier version, friend, but I only bake what's written.

explanations.answer: It will be finished in a day
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't give any timeline like that. Acts 13:41 says God is doing “a work in your days that you would never believe, even if someone told you.” The focus is on the scoffers not believing it. A quick finish is a nice guess, but it isn't in the text.
That's it. Verse 42 says the people urged them to continue this message on the next Sabbath. They don't wait for the door to hit them on the way out, friend. They want more.

Jerusalem came up earlier in the passage, but not here. Verse 42 says the people urged Paul and Barnabas to continue this message on the next Sabbath. They want it right there, in the same place, a week later. Nobody's asking for a trip.

explanations.answer: Write the message on a scroll
explanations.explanation: A scroll is a fine idea, but nobody asks for one. Acts 13:42 says the people urged them to continue this message on the next Sabbath. They want to hear it, in person, again. That's the kind of response that makes a teacher's day.
Grace is right. Verse 43 says Paul and Barnabas spoke to them and urged them to continue in the grace of God. That's the whole send-off, friend, and it's a good one. Grace is the word to hold onto.

The temple is a natural guess, since this crowd knows its worship places. But Acts 13:43 says Paul and Barnabas urged them to continue in the grace of God. The word in the blank is grace. It's good news for the one who doesn't have a building to carry around.

Law is a fair guess, because the crowd just heard the law read and Paul brought it up. But verse 43 says they urged them to continue in the grace of God. Paul said in verse 39 that through Jesus everyone who believes is justified from what the law of Moses couldn't do. So the blank is grace.

Jealousy is right. Verse 45 says when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy. The crowd is big, and some people can't handle it. I think that's a hard thing to see, a good thing happening and somebody sour about it.

Fear is a believable feeling for a moment like this. But Acts 13:45 says they were filled with jealousy when they saw the crowds. The text names the feeling, so I'll go with the text. Fear would be my guess too, friend, but I'm not the one writing this.

Sorrow would make the story softer, but it isn't the word. Verse 45 says when the Jews saw the crowds, “they were filled with jealousy.” Then they contradicted what Paul was saying. The text gives us jealousy, and the rest of the verse follows from it.
That's not how it goes. Verse 46 says Paul and Barnabas answered them boldly. Boldly is the opposite of quiet and careful. Nobody tiptoes in this verse, friend.
False is right. Acts 13:46 says Paul and Barnabas “answered them boldly.” They don't back down, and they don't whisper. They say what needs saying, and they say it out loud.

The Gentiles it is. Verse 46 says, “…we now turn to the Gentiles.” Paul and Barnabas say it was necessary to speak God's word to the Jews first, and then they make the turn. That's the direction of the whole next part.

The synagogue leaders were the ones who invited them to speak in verse 15, so I see the thought. But in Acts 13:46 Paul and Barnabas say, “…we now turn to the Gentiles.” The turn goes to a different group. It's a sharp turn, friend, and the text says it clearly.

Jerusalem comes up in the sermon, so it's an easy one to grab. But Acts 13:46 says Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles. The people of Jerusalem showed up in verse 27 as those who didn't recognize Jesus, not as the next audience. So the answer is the Gentiles.

A light for the Gentiles is right. Verse 47 has the Lord's words: “I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth.” Paul and Barnabas say this is what the Lord commanded them. That's a big job, and it comes from Him.

That phrase is from another part of Scripture, so I see where it came from. But in Acts 13:47 the Lord says, “I have made you a light for the Gentiles…” That's the line Paul and Barnabas quote. The light is the answer.

A shield is a strong picture, but it isn't the one in this verse. Acts 13:47 says, “I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth.” So the answer is a light for the Gentiles. The reach goes to the ends of the earth, friend, which is a long way for a shield.
True. Verse 48 says, “…all who were appointed for eternal life believed.” That's after the Gentiles heard the news and rejoiced. The text states it plainly, and I'll keep it exactly there.

The text says the opposite. Acts 13:48 reads, “…all who were appointed for eternal life believed.” The Gentiles heard it, rejoiced, and glorified the word of the Lord. So the answer lands on True, friend.
Right. Verse 49 says, “And the word of the Lord spread throughout that region.” It starts in a synagogue and goes way past it. That's some serious reach, and it didn't need a group chat.

The word started in the synagogue, but verse 49 says it spread “throughout that region.” It didn't stay put. Not even a locked door keeps good news in, and no walls got mentioned here. So the answer is the region.

explanations.answer: No farther than the city gate
explanations.explanation: That's a short trip for news. But Acts 13:49 says the word of the Lord spread throughout that region. It goes well past the city gate. Good news travels farther than a gate can handle, friend.

explanations.answer: Drives them out of the district
explanations.explanation: Right. Verse 50 says the Jews stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their district. They incited the religious women of prominence and the leading men of the city to get it done. It's a heavy moment, and I think it stings a little.

explanations.answer: Puts them in the city jail
explanations.explanation: Jail doesn't show up in this passage. Acts 13:50 says the persecution drove Paul and Barnabas out of their district. So they're sent out, not locked in. It's a different kind of hard, friend, and the text says it plainly.

The proconsul does come up in Paul's journey, but this verse doesn't use him. Acts 13:50 says the persecution drove Paul and Barnabas out of their district. Nobody's hauled in front of an official here. They just have to go.

Dust is right. Verse 51 says they shook the dust off their feet in protest against them. It's a clear move, no words needed. I know a thing or two about dust, friend, and I've never made a point that good with it.
Iconium is right. Verse 51 says they shook the dust off their feet and went to Iconium. So the road keeps going, and the story goes with it. The journey doesn't stop when one town says no.

Water sounds like something you'd shake off, so I see the idea. But verse 51 says they shook the dust off their feet. Dust is the word that goes in that first blank. Water would be a lot messier on a long road.
Lystra is a real town, but it's not where they go in this verse. Acts 13:51 says they went to Iconium. So Lystra is a good guess for the map, and still not the answer for this blank.
Oil makes a mess, and I'd know, because my apron has met a lot of it. But verse 51 says they shook the dust off their feet. So the word for the first blank is dust. Oil isn't in this verse at all.

True. Verse 52 says, “And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.” That's right after Paul and Barnabas get driven out. The text puts the joy and the Holy Spirit together, and I'll leave it just as it is.

I get why you'd doubt it, after the persecution. But Acts 13:52 says, “And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.” So the passage closes on joy, not gloom. The text says so, friend.
